parameterised by pattern (random, modular, hierarchical) crossed with epistatic
density; the main sweep crosses 2 densities $\times$ 8 rivalry $\times$ 8
imitation values, 10 replications each, for 1{,}280 runs.

**Results.**  Deleting channels from the calibrated model separates them
cleanly.  Terminal $\bar K_{AA}$ at round 100, ten replications per scenario:

| Scenario | $\bar K_{AA}$ | 95\% interval | Fold |
|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline (calibrated) | 0.034 | 0.020--0.052 | 1.00 |
| Imitation removed ($K_{CA} = 0$) | 0.108 | 0.086--0.128 | **3.2** |
| Epistasis removed ($K_{CC} = 0$) | 0.010 | 0.007--0.017 | 0.29 |
| All competition removed | 0.399 | 0.322--0.543 | 11.7 |

Removing imitation *raises* convergence 3.2-fold, and removing epistasis
collapses it by 71 percent.  Under similarity-weighted imitation firms chase
whichever peers resemble them, which disperses them across the space; shared
structure is what concentrates them.  A 54-cell robustness sweep finds the
ordering holds in 27 of 27 hierarchical cells and 17 of 27 modular cells, which
scopes the claim to architectural regime rather than asserting it universally.

![Industry trajectory. Mean pairwise route overlap among U.S. carriers 1993--2025 with era shading and merger markers, the empirical series the simulation is calibrated against.\label{fig:kaatraj}](figures/cd2026_kaa_trajectory.png){width=100%}

**Mode of use, stated plainly.**  This application predates the package.  Its
simulation results come from an independent procedural implementation, and
\pkg{searchnet} enters as a second implementation checked against it.  That
arrangement is worth describing because it is how the package is validated in
practice.  A conformance harness runs nine parameter cells $\times$ three seeds
through both implementations and compares them on three layers: structural
agreement, trajectory hashes, and *invariants* --- the NK reduction of
Theorem 1 (Reduction) and monotonicity of crowding in the rivalry
parameter.  Its design note states the discipline that makes such a comparison
meaningful:

> \pkg{searchnet} is R6 over \pkg{RSiena} and the reference engine is
> procedural, so bit-identical trajectories are *not* expected: the random
> number stream is consumed in a different order.  Reporting a cross-paradigm
> trajectory mismatch as a defect would be a category error.

Structural and invariant layers must agree; trajectory hashes need not.  We
recommend this three-layer split to anyone validating a simulation package
against an existing implementation.

A second discipline this application enforces is worth transferring.  The
potential-game property of Section~\ref{sec:formal-properties} was tested *on
the simulation code* rather than on a reduced model: add an activity, then drop
it, and net utility must return to zero.  It does, to machine precision, for the
core specification.  The same probe *locates* the boundary --- with
similarity-weighted imitation active the path integral deviates by 2.68 at
calibrated coefficients, because that term depends on rivals' performances,
which move when the focal firm moves.  The formal guarantees are therefore
claimed for the core specification only, and the probe is what draws the line.



**Takeaway.**  Convergence is produced by shared structure, not by copying: the
channel whose removal *raises* overlap cannot be the channel generating it.  For
package users, the transferable practice is the three-layer conformance split and
the path-integral probe that marks where a formal guarantee stops.

### Architectural shocks and the rate--evaluation split {#sec:app-shocks}

**Research question.**  When an innovation reshapes which activities complement
which, firms differ in how fast they can respond.  Can the *cost of effecting*
a repositioning be separated from the *value of the destination* using
observational data?  Archival panels record the option taken and never the
options declined, so "did not reposition" is equally consistent with *could not
afford to* and *did not want to*.

**Construct and channels.**  This is the application that exploits the SAOM's
distinctive factorisation.  The rate function $\lambda_i$ governs *how often*
an actor gets to move; the evaluation function $f_i$ governs *where* it moves.
Adjustment cost is a rate quantity and destination value is an evaluation
quantity, so a model that separates them can identify what a single-equation
model cannot.  The design manipulates \code{RateX} alone and holds the
evaluation function *identical* across arms --- the covariate effect is declared
with \code{parameter = 0} precisely so that it is inert.

**Design.**  $M = 12$ actors, $N = 12$ components, 30 iterations per actor (360
ministeps), 20 seed pairs.  $K_{CC}$ shifts mid-run: two \code{XWX} dyadic
covariates carry $W_{\text{pre}}$ and $W_{\text{post}}$, and \code{theta\_shocks}
flips their weights from $(1,0)$ to $(0,1)$ at the midpoint, so the firm's
position carries across the switch and is re-scored under the new structure.

![The $K_{CC}$ switch. Left, the pre-shock influence matrix $W_{\text{pre}}$; centre, the post-shock $W_{\text{post}}$; right, their difference. The shock schedule flips the weights of two \code{XWX} covariates at the midpoint, so actors carry their positions across a change in which components complement which.\label{fig:wswitch}](figures/ishock_w_switch.png){width=100%}

```r
Wpre  <- create_block_diag(N, 2)
Wpost <- create_block_diag(N, 3)

mkm <- function(rateX) {
  rts <- if (rateX == 0) list() else list(
    list(effect = "RateX", parameter = rateX, dv_name = DV, fix = TRUE,
         interaction1 = "self$strat_1_coCovar"))
  list(dv_bipartite = list(name = DV, rates = rts,
    effects = list(
      list(effect = "density", parameter = -0.6, dv_name = DV, fix = TRUE),
      list(effect = "inPop",   parameter = -0.4, dv_name = DV, fix = TRUE)),
    coCovars = list(
      list(effect = "egoX", parameter = 0, dv_name = DV, fix = TRUE,
           interaction1 = "self$strat_1_coCovar", x = grp)),
    coDyadCovars = list(
      list(effect = "XWX", parameter = 1, dv_name = DV, fix = TRUE,
           nodeSet = c("COMPONENTS", "COMPONENTS"),
           interaction1 = "self$component_1_coDyadCovar", x = Wpre),
      list(effect = "XWX", parameter = 0, dv_name = DV, fix = TRUE,
           nodeSet = c("COMPONENTS", "COMPONENTS"),
           interaction1 = "self$component_2_coDyadCovar", x = Wpost))))
}

shocks <- list(
  list(effect_level = c("XWX_1", "XWX_2"), parameter = c(1, 0), portion = 1, shock_on = 0),
  list(effect_level = c("XWX_1", "XWX_2"), parameter = c(0, 1), portion = 1, shock_on = 1))

env <- SaomNkRSienaBiEnv$new(list(M = M, N = N, BI_PROB = 0.3, rand_seed = 7000 + s))
env$search_rsiena(structure_model = mkm(rateX), iterations_per_actor = 30,
                  run_seed = 7000 + s, theta_shocks = shocks)
```

**Results.**  The rate manipulation separates cleanly: with \code{RateX = 2},
quick-to-act actors make 51.0 tie changes against 6.7 for slow-to-act, a ratio
of 7.6, while the control arm sits at 1.05.  Every one of 40 runs shows a
post-shock fitness valley.  Two results are reported as null and should be:
neither valley depth ($p = 0.18$) nor time to trough ($p = 0.50$) differs
between arms.

The substantive finding is a selection wedge.  Comparing movers to
non-movers in the same treated world gives $-0.054$; comparing each mover to its
own matched counterfactual gives $-0.032$; the difference, $-0.022$
($t = -2.46$, $p = 0.015$), is what the observational comparison attributes to
repositioning that is in fact selection.  Notably, applying the *airline*
project's decomposition to the same runs gives a mean wedge of $-0.002$ ---
degenerate, exactly as that decomposition's algebraic identity requires.  Two
conventions, one dataset, opposite informativeness: a reminder that a
decomposition's benchmark determines what it can detect.


![Rate separation. With \code{RateX} active, quick-to-act actors make 51.0 tie changes against 6.7 for slow-to-act (ratio 7.6) while the control arm sits at 1.05, with evaluation functions held identical across arms.\label{fig:rateseparation}](figures/ishock_rate_separation.png){width=100%}

**Takeaway.**  Separating the rate function from the evaluation function turns an
unidentified question --- was the firm unwilling or unable? --- into two estimable
quantities.  A decomposition's benchmark determines what it can detect: the same
runs yield a significant wedge under one convention and a degenerate zero under
another.

### Startup workforce formation {#sec:app-workforce}

**Research question.**  Startups hire to build capability, but breadth carries a
coordination cost.  When does successful co-construction foreclose its own
continuation?  The Penrose Effect predicts an inverted-U between workforce
breadth and performance.

**Construct and channels.**  Actors are startups, components are skills.
Workforce breadth is $K_{AC}$ (\code{outAct}); competition for the same scarce
skills is $K_{CA}$ (\code{inPop}); skill complementarity within a team is
$K_{CC}$, entered as an empirically estimated $W$.  Labour-market overlap
between startups is $K_{AA}$ and is *measured but not driven* --- a good
illustration of the projection channel used as an outcome.

**Design and calibration.**  $M = 50$ startups, $N = 12$ skills, 20 steps per
actor.  The parameters are not chosen; they are \pkg{RSiena} point estimates
from a fitted bipartite SAOM on Crunchbase founding cohorts
(\code{density} $= -1.756$, \code{inPop} $= 0.022$, \code{outAct} $= 0.089$),
carried into simulation through the functional API:

```r
env <- saomnk_env(M = 50, N = 12, density = 0.3, seed = seed)

mod <- saomnk_model(
  density          = -1.756,   # fitted
  popularity       =  0.022,   # fitted (K_CA)
  scope            =  0.089,   # fitted (K_AC)
  influence_matrix = W_emp,    # empirical epistasis (K_CC)
  influence_weight = -0.062)

saomnk_run(env, mod, steps_per_actor = 20L, seed = seed + 7L)
degs <- saomnk_get_degrees(env)   # K_AC, K_CA, K_AA, K_CC read out together
```

![Utility decomposition for the workforce application, separating each actor's objective into its density, scope and epistasis contributions. The scope term is positive at the fitted parameters, which is why no inverted U appears.\label{fig:bortwaterfall}](figures/bort_utility_waterfall.png){width=85%}

**Results, including a negative one.**  Under the calibrated specification the
inverted-U *does not appear*: the quadratic coefficient is positive in all seven
conditions.  The diagnosis is transparent rather than mysterious --- the fitted
\code{outAct} is $+0.089$, so the estimated model contains no scope-cost term,
and a curve with no cost cannot bend down.  Re-specifying with \code{scope} $< 0$
recovers the inverted-U in 8 of 27 cells, and every one of those 8 sits at the
empirical popularity value.  A further design lets the scope cost regenerate
from the realised landscape each wave; the inverted-U appears, but the
emergence ratio is $\approx 0.99$, meaning the curvature passes through from the
imposed cost rather than being generated by feedback.  We report this because it
is the kind of result a simulation package should make easy to obtain and hard
to overstate: the mechanism was not found, and the reason it was not found is
legible in the fitted parameters.


![Workforce application. Left, the $\K$-4 panel for 50 startups over 250 steps, showing all four channels read out together. Right, breadth ($K_{AC}$) against utility; the relationship is monotone and concave, that is diminishing returns, not the inverted U the Penrose Effect predicts.\label{fig:workforce}](figures/bort_k4_panel.png){width=49%}
![](figures/bort_phase_space.png){width=49%}

**Takeaway.**  Calibrating to fitted coefficients rather than to chosen ones makes
a simulation falsifiable, and here it falsified the expected result: no inverted U
appears because the fitted scope term is positive, so the model contains no
coordination cost to bend the curve.

### Policy shocks and risk-taking {#sec:app-policy}

**Research question.**  When a government subsidy arrives and later withdraws,
do treated firms shift toward exploratory activity, and does the shift persist
once the support is removed?

**Construct and channels.**  A subsidy is modelled as a timed change in an
actor-covariate effect rather than as a change in the landscape: eligible firms
receive a positive \code{egoX} weight, together with interactions on scope
(\code{outAct|egoX}) that make the subsidy's effect depend on how broad the
firm already is.  $K_{CC}$ carries the exploration structure through \code{XWX}
with a component risk matrix.  The design exercises \pkg{searchnet}'s shock
schedule in its three-regime form --- pre-policy, policy, post-policy --- which
is the natural way to represent a temporary intervention:

```r
theta_shocks <- list(
  list(effect_level = c("egoX", "outAct|egoX_1", "outActSqrt|egoX_2"),
       parameter = c(0, 0, 0),             portion = pre_portion,    shock_on = 0),
  list(effect_level = c("egoX", "outAct|egoX_1", "outActSqrt|egoX_2"),
       parameter = c(1, h1_val, h2_val),   portion = policy_portion, shock_on = 1),
  list(effect_level = c("egoX", "outAct|egoX_1", "outActSqrt|egoX_2"),
       parameter = c(0, 0, 0),             portion = post_portion,   shock_on = 0))

env <- SaoMNK$new(list(M = M, N = N, init_matrix = init_matrix))
env$search_rsiena(structure_model = structure_model,
                  theta_shocks    = theta_shocks,
                  iterations_per_actor = n_iterations_per_actor * env$N,
                  run_seed = run_seed)
```

**Design.**  $M = 18$ firms, $N = 16$ components, 64 iterations per actor; a
$6 \times 5 \times 4 \times 3$ parameter grid of 360 cells at five seeds each,
for 1{,}800 simulations.

**What the package supplies.**  The risk-taking trajectory and
exploration--exploitation plots are produced by \pkg{searchnet}'s own plotting
layer from the simulated chain, not by bespoke code, which is the intended
division of labour: the package computes the actor-level series and the analyst
supplies the contrast.  We show the trajectory panel rather than the
difference-in-differences panel, because the latter's period axis is ordered
lexically rather than temporally --- a reminder that a plot returned by a
package is still the analyst's responsibility to read.


![Policy shock. Actor-level risk-taking trajectories for subsidised and control firms across the three-regime shock schedule, plotted by \pkg{searchnet} from the simulated chain; the vertical line marks the policy onset.\label{fig:policyshock}](figures/amr_risk_trajectories.png){width=100%}

**Takeaway.**  A temporary intervention is naturally expressed as a three-regime
shock schedule, and the package's plotting layer returns actor-level series ready
for the contrast the analyst chooses.

### Firm and industry effects {#sec:app-variance}

The variance-decomposition literature asks whether firm or industry effects
explain more of the variance in profitability.  If firms are competitively
coupled, the two are not separable in principle, and a simulation in which the
data-generating process is known can show what a decomposition recovers.

This application is the cleanest illustration of the minimal functional
pipeline, and we present it as such:

```r
env <- saomnk_env(M = M, N = N, density = 0.2, seed = seed)
K   <- make_influence_matrix(N, arch_type)      # modular | hierarchical | random

mod <- saomnk_model(density = -0.5, popularity = coupling,
                    scope = 0.05, influence_matrix = K, influence_weight = 0.1)

saomnk_run(env, mod, steps_per_actor = 15L, seed = seed + 1L)
bi_mat <- saomnk_get_bipartite(env)
```

Coupling strength enters through \code{popularity}, sweeping $\{0, 0.1, 0.3,
0.5, 0.8\}$ across three architectures.  We report the pipeline, not a bias
estimate: in the present implementation the "true" effects are re-derived from
the same realised performance the estimator sees, so the recovered bias is zero
by construction.  Establishing a bias requires taking the truth from the
generating parameters instead, and that work is ongoing.  We state this because
a software paper is the wrong place to launder an unfinished result, and because
the pipeline above is genuinely the shortest path from a specification to a
simulated bipartite panel.

**Takeaway.**  The shortest path from specification to simulated panel is four
calls.  The vignette also shows what a simulation cannot do for you: if the
"true" effects are re-derived from the same realised outcome the estimator sees,
recovered bias is zero by construction, whatever the coupling.

### Market-access institutions {#sec:app-international}

**Research question.**  Do institutional distances between countries act as
tolls on entry, or as topology that reshapes which markets are complementary?
A toll shifts the cost of a market; topology changes what a market is worth
*given what else the firm holds* --- and the two are separable, because the
first is a main effect on the component and the second is $K_{CC}$.

**Design.**  A bipartite firm-by-market panel: 534 firms $\times$ 63 markets
$\times$ 4 waves, 8{,}023 ties, with nine coupling matrices built from CEPII
gravity data and United Nations voting-similarity scores.  Each matrix enters
*twice* --- once as a component main effect and once as \code{XWX} --- so the
two mechanisms compete for the same variance in one model.

![Post-estimation use. Left, a geographic network view produced by \code{saomnk\_plot\_geo\_network()}. Right, a specification curve built with \pkg{searchnet}'s estimate-extraction and scaled-autocorrelation helpers over \pkg{RSiena} fits; these functions existed but were unreachable without \code{:::} until the \code{NAMESPACE} was corrected in 0.6.0.\label{fig:intl}](figures/intl_geo_network.png){width=49%}
![](figures/intl_spec_curve.png){width=49%}

**Mode of use and result.**  Estimation runs through \pkg{RSiena} directly;
\pkg{searchnet} is used for the specification curve and network visualisation.
Both channels operate: a block Wald test gives $\chi^2 = 169.4$ for coupling
against $143.9$ for the main effects, both on 10 degrees of freedom.  An
earlier and stronger claim --- that institutions are topology *rather than*
toll --- was withdrawn after review found the cost-shifting term had been
operationalised as a country-constant row mean while coupling was firm-varying,
which is not a fair contest.  The surviving claim is the weaker and better
supported one, that the distance literature is incomplete rather than
misspecified.

**Takeaway.**  Entering each matrix twice, as a component main effect and as a
coupling term, lets two rival mechanisms compete for the same variance in one
model instead of being compared across models.

### Refactor candidates {#sec:app-refactor}

Two further studies are built on the $\K$ formulation but implement it in bespoke
code.  We include them because the capability each would need is specific and
short, and naming it is more useful to a prospective user than omitting the case.

**Evaluator discipline under capital abundance.**  *Problematization:* when
capital becomes abundant, which margins of organizational evaluation adjust, and
what insulates the rest?  Investors are actors and technology categories are
components, so an investor's portfolio is a bipartite row and complementarity
between categories is exactly $K_{CC}$.  *Methods:* a bipartite SAOM on 368
investors $\times$ 45 categories over six waves, with \code{outActSqrt},
\code{inPopSqrt} and \code{cycle4}, plus complementarity entering as a
*time-varying actor-by-component* covariate interacted with a policy-regime
indicator.  The regime interaction is strongly negative, indicating that
complementarity weighs less in commitment decisions when capital is cheap.
*Takeaway:* the substantive finding is a $K_{CC}$ result, but it is not currently
expressed as one.  *Capability required:* the study needs a **time-varying $W$**
--- \code{varDyadCovar} rather than \code{coDyadCovar} --- so that epistasis can
shift across waves.  Version 0.7.0 supplies this as the \code{influence\_arrays}
argument to \code{saomnk\_model}, covering specification and simulation;
estimation and visualisation of a time-varying $W$ remain open.  The analysis
reported here predates that release and uses hand-built covariate arrays.

**Basin geometry under policy regimes.**  *Problematization:* policy archetypes
that produce indistinguishable average fitness may still leave firms in very
differently shaped basins, and it is the shape, not the height, that determines
what a shock does.  *Methods:* 20 firms and 16 activities across 27 conditions
crossing epistatic density, interaction pattern and erosion, with a ten-term
utility whose scope, synergy, herding and congestion terms are $\K$ channels
written out longhand, and \pkg{RSiena} estimates supplying the coefficients.
*Takeaway:* archetypes converge on fitness --- a spread of 0.18 percent across
four archetypes --- while diverging by roughly an order of magnitude on
hysteresis area.  Fitness parity conceals geometric divergence, which is an
argument for reporting basin shape alongside performance.  *Capability required:*
\pkg{searchnet} already computes fitness landscapes and basin statistics
(Section~\ref{sec:basins}); what is missing is a **tournament driver** that runs
heterogeneous strategy populations against one another and returns ranked
outcomes.  With that, the ten-term utility collapses into a \code{saomnk\_model}
call plus a scoring function.

We flag one caution these two cases share.  Both were written before the package
matured, and both re-implement channels the package now provides.  A reader
adopting \pkg{searchnet} should expect the reverse migration to be the common
case: the framework is easier to express in the package than to re-derive, and
the value of doing so is that the $\K$ channels then carry their standard
meanings rather than local ones.

### Failure modes inherited from \pkg{RSiena} {#sec:app-failures}

Because \pkg{searchnet} delegates estimation to \code{siena07}, it inherits that
estimator's failure modes, and users should know two of them.

The first is provable.  Under method-of-moments estimation, no effect whose
observed statistic lies exactly on the boundary of its attainable support can
converge: the estimate diverges as $\theta \to \pm\infty$.  In a *balanced*
bipartite panel every actor holds at least one component in every wave, so the
isolate count is exactly zero and \code{outTrunc(1)} is exactly $M$ --- both
saturated.  A demonstration on public data changes only the sampling rule: on a
balanced construction \code{outIso} estimates $-18.65$ (SE $6.62$), a runaway;
on an unbalanced construction of the same network, where 1{,}547 of 1{,}316
actor-waves are isolates, it estimates $+3.29$ (SE $0.42$).  The screen is one
line --- compute $(\text{observed} - \text{lo}) / (\text{hi} - \text{lo})$ and
refuse exactly $0$ or $1$ --- and it costs nothing to run before estimating.  We
note that a stronger version of this claim, covering *near*-boundary statistics,
was tested and refuted: only exact saturation disqualifies.

![Why an exactly saturated statistic cannot converge. In a balanced panel the observed isolate count sits on the boundary of its support, so method of moments can match it only as $\theta \to -\infty$; the same network sampled to permit entry and exit puts the statistic in the interior and the effect estimates cleanly.\label{fig:boundary}](figures/remedies_boundary.png){width=100%}

The second is a silent-failure pattern rather than a theorem, and it bit this
package.  \code{RSiena::includeEffects} matches effect names by non-standard
evaluation, so passing a name held in a variable silently selects nothing.  A
version of \pkg{searchnet} passed \code{shortName = eff\$effect} into \code{...},
where the unevaluated expression was deparsed and no effect matched; because the
call was wrapped in \code{tryCatch(..., error = function(e) warning(...))}, the
simulation continued with the covariate effect *absent*.  Every actor-covariate
effect was affected, so results labelled "heterogeneous strategies" were in fact
homogeneous-actor results.  The package now ships a regression test asserting
that every effect declared in a \code{structure\_model} appears with
\code{include == TRUE} in the fitted effects object.  The design lesson
generalises beyond this package: \code{tryCatch}-to-warning is right for
interactive exploration and wrong for a simulation engine whose output gets
published.


# Summary and future directions {#sec:conclusion}

\pkg{searchnet} provides an \proglang{R} package that bridges two established
research traditions---NK fitness landscapes from strategy and organization
theory, and stochastic actor-oriented models from social network
analysis---through a bipartite network reformulation of the search environment.
The package makes three contributions to the computational social science
toolkit.

First, it **endogenizes the fitness landscape**.  By representing the search
environment as a bipartite network governed by a SAOM, landscape ruggedness
becomes an emergent property of actors' affiliation decisions rather than an
exogenously imposed parameter.  Researchers studying adaptation, competitive
dynamics, or organizational design can now model settings where the landscape
itself is shaped by the actors who navigate it.

Second, it **decomposes $K$** into a four-dimensional coupled degree system.
The $\K$ framework reveals that the conventional complexity parameter is one
dimension of a structurally coupled process linking actor behavior to landscape
topology.  The framework does not introduce new network statistics; its
contribution is interpretive, providing a theoretical bridge between the NK
and bipartite network literatures that makes visible the transmission mechanism
through which strategic choices propagate into environmental structure.

Third, it provides a **complete simulation and analysis toolkit**.  The
functional API (\code{saomnk\_env}, \code{saomnk\_model}, \code{saomnk\_run})
lowers the barrier to entry for management scholars unfamiliar with \pkg{RSiena}
syntax.  The $\K$-4 panel, 3D phase space visualization, utility
decomposition, network snapshots, and specification robustness diagnostics
equip researchers with the tools needed to design, execute, and validate
computational experiments.  The package ships with eight vignettes, 16 Manim
animation scenes, a 100-step formal proof chain (Parts A--L, including
Theorem 5's Brock--Durlauf recovery), 300 unit tests, and
interactive game and classroom modules that make the framework accessible to
students and practitioners.

Several directions for future development are planned.  First, integration with
\pkg{RSiena}'s estimation machinery will allow researchers to fit the SaoMNK
model to observed bipartite network panel data, enabling empirical calibration
of simulation parameters.  Second, the fitness landscape module will be
extended with scalable approximation methods (e.g., Walsh decomposition,
landscape correlation analysis) to support problem sizes beyond $N = 20$.
Third, a \pkg{Shiny} dashboard is under development to provide an interactive
visual interface for simulation design and exploration, lowering the adoption
barrier for researchers without programming experience.  Fourth, a web API via
\pkg{plumber} will enable integration with external frontends and
cross-platform deployment.  Two initially planned future directions have
already been realized in the current release: the strategy game mode
(Section~\ref{sec:interactive}) provides gamified engagement with the
framework, and the classroom teaching module offers a Capsim-style
instructional platform with industry presets, AI opponents, and automated
debrief generation.  The accompanying PDW workshop vignette
(\code{vignette("saomnk-pdw-workshop")}) provides a complete three-hour
curriculum for introducing the framework to strategy and organization
scholars.

A companion paper \citep{downing2026architecture} applies the SaoMNK framework
empirically, using eight data layers from U.S.\ airline competitive dynamics to
demonstrate how the $\K$ decomposition reveals structural mechanisms invisible
to the classical scalar $K$ parameterization.

\pkg{searchnet} is available from GitHub at
\url{https://github.com/sdownin/searchnet} and is under preparation for CRAN
submission.  The package requires \proglang{R} $\geq$ 4.1.0 and depends on
\pkg{R6}, \pkg{RSiena}, \pkg{igraph}, \pkg{ggplot2}, \pkg{dplyr},
\pkg{Matrix}, \pkg{network}, and \pkg{reshape2}.
